title: Merchant of Record vs PayFac vs White Label: Choosing a Model for Your Platform
summary:
Most payment teams can open a dashboard in seconds. Fewer can say which number on it would make them change a routing rule today. That gap separates payment analytics that describes the business from payment analytics that runs it.
The role has already moved towards the second kind. In our analysis of 112 Payment Manager job descriptions, reporting and analytics were the most frequently mentioned responsibility, appearing 69% more often than PSP management. The same research shows how much of that analysis still happens by hand: approval rates and declines reconciled across PSPs in spreadsheets, because each provider reports them differently.
In customer success, the dashboard conversation comes up early with almost every team, usually about which charts deserve a place on the screen people open every morning. This column is my answer: the short list of metrics that drive payment decisions, the groundwork that makes payment data comparable, and how often each number deserves a look.
What belongs on payment analytics dashboard (and what doesn't)
Gross merchandise value, transaction count, and total revenue belong in every board pack. On an operational payment analytics dashboard, they mostly add noise. They move with demand, marketing, and seasonality, and a drop in them rarely tells the payment team what to change.
A practical test for every chart: can you name the decision it informs, the person who owns that decision, and the threshold at which they act? If any answer is missing, the metric belongs in a monthly report, not on the screen your team works from.
Two more conditions turn a number into a signal:
Baseline. An 87% approval rate means little on its own, but against the same window yesterday and last week, it shows whether something is moving.
Right cut. A total across all providers hides the provider that caused the problem, so most metrics below are worth reading per provider and per payment method before anything else.
7 payment metrics to track, and the decision each one drives
The metrics below move from whether payments get through to what each one costs and risks.
Approval rate by provider and payment method
This is still the anchor metric, and approval rate is the KPI employers name most often in Payment Manager job descriptions. I covered how to define and lift it in a separate column on improving approval rates across several PSPs. For analytics, one rule matters most: track first-attempt and final approval separately, so cascading and retries do not mask a weakening primary route. The decision it drives is routing priority.
Decline mix: soft, hard, technical, and rule-based
Approval rate shows how much volume failed. Decline mix shows what kind of failure it was, which determines who fixes it. Group declines into four buckets: issuer soft declines, which are recoverable through a retry or a second route; hard declines, which no retry will fix; technical errors on the provider or integration side; and blocks from your own fraud rules or failed authentication. A growing share of technical errors on one provider is an escalation. A growing share of rule-based blocks is a conversation with your risk team. The anatomy of a declined transaction explains why these buckets need different fixes.
Payment method conversion rate
This is the share of attempts on each method that end in a completed payment. For alternative payment methods, much of the loss happens before any provider responds: a redirect the customer abandons, a banking app that times out, a QR code nobody scans. Method conversion catches problems that approval rate never sees. The decision it drives is which methods to show, in what order, and through which provider.
Provider health: failed, pending, and slow transactions
Failure share is the obvious signal. Pending share is the underrated one. A transaction stuck without a final status is neither revenue nor a decline. It generates support tickets, and a queue of pending payments often exposes a provider-side problem before failures do. Track how many transactions are pending, how long the oldest have been waiting, and how provider response times compare with their usual level. The decision here is fast: shift traffic and open an incident with the provider.
Payout success and provider balances
For marketplaces, trading platforms, and any business that pays out, a failed payout is a support case and a trust problem. A payout that cannot leave because a provider balance ran dry is worse, because it was predictable. Track payout success rate per provider and how each balance moves compared with the previous day and week. Then rebalance funds or reroute payouts before the gap appears.
Chargeback and fraud ratios
Chargeback rate and fraud rate both rank among the most frequently named KPIs in the job descriptions we analyzed. Card scheme monitoring programs set ratio limits per merchant, and acquirers often apply stricter internal limits. The useful view is each ratio per merchant account, plotted against the nearest threshold, with a trend line. Decide whether to tighten rules or move risky segments before a monitoring program makes that decision for you.
Cost per successful payment
Rate cards compare providers on transaction price. Payment analytics should compare them on what you pay for each payment that actually completes: all fees, including fixed fees charged on declined attempts, FX margins, and scheme pass-throughs, divided by successful payments. Then read that figure next to the approval rate, because the cheapest route per success is not always the most profitable.
A simplified example shows why. Take 1,000 attempts of $50 split between two providers with the same fixed fee per attempt:

Provider B costs eight cents more per successful payment, yet it completes 70 more payments and returns $3.36 more per attempt after fees. Judged on its rate card, B loses. Judged on revenue per attempt, it wins clearly. That pairing of metrics is what turns a provider review from a pricing debate into a business case.
How to compare payment data across multiple PSPs
Analytics is only as reliable as the payment data behind it, and data from several providers isn't comparable by default. Our research points to inconsistent error codes between providers as one reason cross-PSP comparison still lives in spreadsheets. Four pieces of groundwork fix most of it:
One status model. Map every provider's statuses into one set, so 'successful', 'failed', and 'pending' mean the same thing across your stack.
One decline taxonomy. Translate provider-specific response codes into the decline buckets above. Without this step, you can't compare decline mix across providers.
One clock. Calculate daily and weekly figures in your organization's time zone. Otherwise, a 'bad day' can be a side effect of a provider's UTC cut-off.
One definition per metric. Decide whether approval rate counts attempts or payments, which currency totals report in, and keep those definitions fixed.
This is the least visible part of payment analytics and the one most often skipped. It is also what lets a team trust a chart enough to act on it without first checking the provider's back office.
How often to review each payment metric
Not every metric needs the same attention. Provider failures and pending queues change within minutes and call for alerts. Approval rate, balances, and payout success suit a daily check. Decline mix, method conversion, and dispute ratios show their patterns over a week. Cost per successful payment and provider scorecards need a month of data to support a renegotiation or a change in the provider mix. Each rhythm also has a different owner, which is why a single payment analytics dashboard rarely serves everyone well.

A fair objection: a merchant with one provider in one market does not need seven metrics on day one. Approval rate, decline mix, and cost per successful payment cover most of the decisions this setup enables. The rest earns its place as providers and methods are added, which is when the cost of not seeing a problem early grows fastest. Our payment maturity research found that only 23.9% of businesses use complex operational functionality, including refunds, chargeback management, and analytics, so many teams are still building this layer.
Final thought
Start by removing. List every chart your team looks at and write next to each one the decision it informs. Anything without an answer moves to a report. Then fix comparability, so the remaining numbers mean the same thing across providers, and agree on who checks what, and how often.

title: French Bank Crédit Mutuel Arkéa Loses $133M Through Supplier Breach
summary:
French cooperative bank Crédit Mutuel Arkéa has confirmed it was hit by a cyber attack which saw criminals move $133 million out of the bank after they gained access through a service provider platform.
The attackers used Arkéa’s own account to send funds to other banks, where the money was converted into cryptocurrency.
The banking group, which holds €211.5 billion in assets and serves over 5.8 million customers, temporarily suspended some transactions once the attack was detected.
The theft was first reported on November 2, when blockchain investigator ZachXBT flagged more than $106 million withdrawn from centralised exchange accounts by an unnamed EU entity.
Andy Ward, SVP International for Absolute Security, commented: “Suppliers are often the easiest route in for attackers to cause huge damage to large organisations like Crédit Mutuel Arkéa. AI has shifted the balance of power towards cybercriminals in the short term, helping them to launch attacks at scale and making major breaches a case of when, not if.”
“Financial services will always be a prime target due to the money involved, but the wider concern is the growing pattern of attacks against French organisations, from supermarkets to blood banks, highlighting how cyber threats are increasingly affecting a broad range of industries and the essential services people rely on every day.”
“These attacks should serve as a warning for businesses to bolster their cyber defences, which starts with knowing which devices and supplier systems can reach their networks. Over half of CISOs reported facing a cyber breach over the past year, according to our research, with recovery costing an average of $2.5m per incident. Having the ability to recover from cyber attacks quickly and reduce downtime is vital.”
The bank has not named the supplier involved but has ruled out Fortuneo, which had been linked to the attack in the French media. The breach has been described as a sophisticated external attack and has warned customers to expect a rise in phishing attempts.
The attack follows a wave of attacks on French organisations. France formally blamed a unit of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps for October's attacks on refrigeration systems at around 700 supermarkets, summoning the Iranian ambassador and calling for EU sanctions. Refrigeration systems at three French blood-storage facilities were also targeted though that attack has not been attributed.

title: The Payments Association Launches Payments Manifesto Setting Out UK Priorities to 2030
summary:
The Payments Association, a trade group representing the payments sector, has published The Payments Manifesto 2027, setting out a national strategy for trusted, competitive and innovative payments by 2030. The manifesto calls for payments to be recognised as critical national infrastructure, alongside sectors such as energy, telecommunications and transport.   
Aimed at government, regulators and industry leaders, the Manifesto draws on engagement with The Payments Association’s membership and has been reviewed by its Advisory Board. It builds on the Government’s National Payments Vision, setting out practical priorities to support progress towards 2030. 
The Payments Manifesto 2027: A national strategy for trusted, competitive and innovative payments by 2030 is structured around four interconnected national objectives.  
Growth, Competitiveness and Resilience focuses on modernising UK payments infrastructure through interoperability and resilience, while creating the conditions for payments businesses to grow and compete internationally.  
Trust, Security and Consumer Protection calls for earlier fraud prevention through intelligence sharing and accountability across the fraud chain, alongside improvements in financial inclusion, capability and meaningful payment choice.  
AI, Data and Digital Infrastructure seeks trusted rules for secure and accountable agentic payments, supported by internationally interoperable standards for agentic commerce.  
The future of Money and Payments calls for coherent, proportionate and internationally interoperable regulation for next-generation payments, including stablecoins and tokenised money.  
Nick Kerigan, Chair of The Payments Association’s Advisory Board and Managing Director, Head of Innovation at Swift, emphasised that payments are the invisible infrastructure of the UK economy. He highlighted that the Manifesto combines policy recommendations with The Payments Association’s commitment to convene expertise, build evidence and test proposals against real market experience. He also pointed to the Manifesto’s proposal on agentic commerce, interoperability and earlier fraud prevention as examples of how industry collaboration can help strengthen the UK’s payments sector by 2030. 
Emma Banymandhub, CEO of The Payments Association, said: “The assumption that payments can run on autopilot while facing mounting fraud and digital disruption has to end. Payments are the vital economic lifeblood keeping society functioning. If money stopped moving for even five minutes, the fallout would be significant. We aren't just presenting a wish list. Our members are stepping up to deliver the accountability, infrastructure and cross-sector collaboration required to future-proof the UK economy." 
Renuka Rawlins, Director of Policy and Government Relations at The Payments Association, commented: “The challenge now is turning policy ambition into practical progress. This Manifesto identifies where industry, government and regulators need to work together to deliver meaningful change. The Payments Association will help convene that collaboration, develop the evidence needed to inform decisions and track progress against the priorities as we work towards 2030.” 
The Manifesto’s eight policy recommendations cover the modernisation of UK payments infrastructure; international competitiveness for payments businesses; earlier fraud prevention through actionable intelligence sharing; financial inclusion and meaningful payment choice; trusted rules for agentic payments; internationally interoperable standards for agentic commerce; proportionate regulation for next-generation payments; and interoperability between existing and emerging forms of regulated money.

title: European Founders Trust AI Providers More Than Their Governments to Drive Growth
summary:
European founders trust AI providers and sales platforms more than their own governments to support their growth, according to new research from issuer processing powerhouse Enfuce.
The findings point to a trust gap at the heart of Europe's startup economy: the institutions with the most power over founders' growth are the ones they trust least.
The Startup Trust Index asked 700 founders across the UK, France, Germany, Italy, Spain and the Nordics how much they trust, depend on and feel the power of 14 types of organisation, from banks and investors to software providers and government.
Key findings
37% of founders highly trust AI providers to support their growth, compared with 27% for government, the lowest of the 14 organisation types tested
Governments also rank first for power: 38% say their own government has high power over their growth, rising to 47% in the UK
56% depend on at least one type of organisation they have limited trust in, and 30% of them say the reason is lack of suitable alternatives
69% of founders use AI, and among them 56% report higher productivity and 52% better revenue or margins
Only 41% of founders are confident Europe is a good place to build and scale a business, and 39% have considered relocating, incorporating or raising outside Europe
Governments hold the power, but tech providers earn more trust 
Founders across Europe see their government as the organisation with the most power over their growth. Yet only 27% say they strongly trust it, the lowest of any organisation in the survey.
Founders put far more faith in investors and the technology and commercial partners they work with every day. AI providers and sales and distribution platforms are the most trusted, each rated highly by 37% of founders, followed by investors (35%). Other technology providers also outscore government, including business software providers (34%) and cloud infrastructure providers (32%).
The gap is biggest in the UK. Almost half of UK founders (47%) say the government has a lot of power over their growth, but fewer than a quarter (24%) strongly trust it.
AI is fuelling startup growth 
AI is becoming an established part of startup operations, with 69% of founders using it in their business, with 19% using it also for business-critical decisions and processes. One in four identify using AI as one of the developments that most supported their growth over the past year. 
Founders’ confidence in AI is grounded in ROI, with 56% reporting increased productivity and 52% reporting improved revenue or profit margins. Across all founders, 58% agree that AI presents a bigger opportunity than a threat to their business. 
Still, technology only goes so far. Almost two in three founders (63%) say the relationships they have built matter more to their growth than the technology they use.
Limited choice leaves startups reliant on partners they don’t fully trust 
More than half of founders (56%) depend on at least one type of organisation they have limited trust in. Three in ten of them (30%) say there is simply no suitable alternative. Others say the organisation gives them capabilities they can't easily get elsewhere (28%), or that the benefits outweigh their concerns (26%).
Founders rely most on sales and distribution platforms, with 35% rating their dependence on them highly. Investors (32%) and traditional retail banks (31%) come next.
What earns their trust is practical. Asked what makes them trust an organisation to support their growth, founders put value for money and keeping promises joint first (36% each), followed by being clear about terms, charges and decisions (32%).
This is the challenge for Europe's startup ecosystem. Founders need partners they can depend on, but with few alternatives, many end up relying on organisations they don't fully trust.
Growth ambitions collide with economic pressures
Operating costs were the most common barrier to growth over the past year, cited by 32% of founders, followed by economic or policy uncertainty (29%). Looking ahead, two in five founders (42%) name lower operating costs as one of the changes that would help them grow most, rising to half (50%) in the UK.
But founders aren't building just to sell. Asked what success would look like in five years, only 17% mention a sale or public listing. Far more want to build a durable, independent business, grow their revenue and customer base, or achieve financial security for themselves and their families (39% each).
“Europe’s founders trust AI providers more than their own governments to help them grow. Europe’s governments should take that seriously if they want the next generation of great companies built here,” said Denise Johansson, CEO and Co-Founder at Enfuce. “And the stakes are about to rise. AI is moving from helping founders work to making decisions, including payments, on their behalf. When something goes wrong, founders will want to know exactly who answers for it. Technology can be copied. Trust has to be earned.”

title: Sage partners with Adyen and Mastercard to deliver business accounts with debit cards for small busi
summary:
Sage, the leader in accounting, financial, HR and payroll technology for small and mid-sized businesses (SMBs), today announced at Sage Future for Partners Amsterdam partnerships with Mastercard and Adyen, the global financial technology platform of choice for leading brands, as it develops integrated financial services for small businesses across the European markets where Sage operates. Mastercard will serve as Sage's card network partner, supporting debit card capabilities within the service, while Adyen will provide Banking-as-a-Service infrastructure and onboarding for the first implementation in France.
Across Europe, small businesses are running their finances across a growing number of tools.
Accounting software is now one part of a wider financial stack, and new e-invoicing and digital reporting requirements are arriving market by market. Sage is developing services that bring banking, payments and reconciliation into the software small businesses already use, starting with France and expanding across its European markets.
That growing complexity is reflected in Mastercard research, which shows that European SMEs use five digital business tools on average, with 70% saying integrated tools are critical to their business. By connecting banking services with accounting workflows, Sage aims to reduce the need for businesses to move between systems, re-enter information and reconcile transactions separately.
“Small businesses shouldn't have to move between separate systems to manage their finances,” said Derk Bleeker, Chief Commercial Officer, Sage. “We're developing services that bring more of those everyday activities into the software they already use to run their business. This is the first implementation of our broader European Banking-as-a-Service strategy and an important step in helping customers manage more of their financial activity through Sage.”
Bringing financial operations into one place
Small businesses often use separate systems to manage accounting records, make payments, monitor company spending and reconcile transactions. Moving between those systems can create additional administration, duplicate effort and make it harder to maintain an accurate, up-to-date view of their financial position.
Research from Oliver Wyman found that 53% of SMBs surveyed across France, Germany and the Netherlands identified accounting and ERP software as their preferred platform for accessing embedded finance products, while 64% planned to use new or additional embedded finance products through their software provider within the following 12 months.
Designed to complement customers’ existing banking relationships, the service will bring together business account, debit card, payment and reconciliation capabilities within Sage software.
When bank accounts and debit cards live inside Sage, everyday banking happens seamlessly in the background. Books update automatically as money moves, reducing the need to move between separate systems and giving businesses a real-time view of their cash position instead of yesterday’s snapshot.
“Small businesses are at their best when they can focus their time and energy on growing their business, not navigating fragmented financial tools,” said Mark Barnett, Global Head of Small and Medium Enterprises at Mastercard. “By bringing payments and financial services directly into the Sage experience, we’re helping make everyday financial management simpler and more connected. Starting in Europe, we see an opportunity to bring this more connected approach to small businesses around the world.”
Bringing Banking-as-a-Service to Sage customers
The first implementation is planned for Sage 50, Sage 100 and Sage Active in France, with Adyen providing Banking-as-a-Service infrastructure and onboarding. Sage expects its approach and provider arrangements to vary across markets as it develops the strategy across Europe.
Customers will be able to make payments, manage company spending using debit cards and keep banking activity connected with their accounting in Sage. The service is designed to complement customers' existing banking relationships rather than replace them.
Bringing banking services and accounting workflows together also strengthens the proposition Sage partners can take to customers, giving small businesses more of the capabilities they need through a connected financial experience.
"Financial services belong within the platforms businesses already use," said Nicole Olbe, President, EMEA at Adyen. "The future of finance is embedded. By powering Sage with Adyen’s Banking-as-a-Service infrastructure, we are providing the enterprise-grade engine that makes this possible, allowing Sage to transform its software into a comprehensive financial hub where small businesses can manage accounts, payments, and reconciliation all in one place."

title: DoorID Launches to Tackle AI Identity Fraud at the Front Door
summary:
A driving licence photo can be altered in 28 seconds using freely available AI. DoorID checks something much harder to fake: a real person, at a real address, in real time.
DoorID launches today to help lenders and other businesses check that a customer can physically access the address they have given, at the moment it matters most: before money or goods change hands.
Founded by Paul Williams with his brother and co-founder, Iain Williams, DoorID uses a guided smartphone check to connect a person to a property. It adds live evidence of physical access alongside existing identity and fraud checks.
Customers receive a link and complete a guided check via their own phone’s browser. The check takes about 70 seconds, with no app to download. The check brings together identity, location presence, capture integrity and property evidence. On completion, DoorID returns a ‘Pass’, ‘Refer’ or ‘Fail’ result with a tamper-evident evidence pack. Businesses choose where the check sits in their onboarding journey, such as before releasing funds. Verification data is handled in line with UK GDPR.
The idea for DoorID came from an unexpected source. A genuine customer of Quick Car Finance, the brothers’ Bournemouth-based car finance brokerage, which employs around 60 people, was away on holiday when asked for a photo check. Instead, she sent an AI-generated image of an open front door. It looked real, but Paul spotted that something was off.
Paul Williams, founder of DoorID, said: “She was a genuine customer who simply wasn’t at home, and she’d used AI to make a picture of an open door. If someone would do that for convenience, we had to ask what a determined fraudster would do.”
He added: “Documents can carry the right name and address without proving that the person can get through the front door. The answer isn’t more hassle for every customer or more cumbersome onboarding. It’s intelligent friction: one quick check at the moment the risk is real, which protects genuine customers as much as the business.”
The launch follows a demonstration in which the team used a freely available AI tool to change the photograph on a driving licence image in 28 seconds. The exercise illustrates how easily AI can manipulate the visual evidence in an identity document. It was not a test of whether the altered image would pass a lender’s checks.
During the first half of 2026, Cifas recorded more than 220,000 fraud-risk cases on the UK National Fraud Database, its highest January–June total. Identity fraud accounted for 59% of cases, rising 9% year on year to nearly 130,000. Impersonation using a victim’s current address remained the leading reason for identity-fraud filings and increased by 12% compared with the same period in 2025.
The brothers’ experience comes from running Quick Car Finance, which they started after helping their mother find a car and arrange finance. The brokerage has been trading for nine years. Paul built DoorID, drawing on that first-hand knowledge of customer journeys and fraud risk.
DoorID has been tested through Quick Car Finance. It is designed for any business that needs to know a customer can really get to the address they’ve given, including banks, mortgage lenders, conveyancers, asset and device finance providers, telecoms providers, insurers and housing providers.

title: Singles' Day Data Shows Retail Lift in Asia-Pacific and UK, Signalling Merchant Trends for 2026
summary:
Payments data from Checkout.com, a leading global payments company, shows that Singles' Day 2025 lifted online spend across Asia-Pacific retail and UK fashion and general retail. The figures give merchants an early indication of where demand may build as the peak-shopping season begins this year.
Originating in China, Singles' Day takes place annually on 11 November, with consumers celebrating singlehood. It is now the first major event of the peak season, ahead of Black Friday on 27 November.
Checkout.com compared payments on Singles' Day 2025 with the daily average of the seven days before it. Spend with Asia-Pacific merchants was 16% higher than on a normal day*, the clearest event-driven spike in the data.
Retail drove that lift with department store spending rising 70% in Asia-Pacific, general retail spending rising about 20%, and clothing rising 16%. Together, these three categories were up almost 25%, compared with 4% for the same categories outside Asia-Pacific. 
In the UK, compared with the previous Tuesday (4 November 2025), Singles' Day spend was 31% higher in general retail, 23% higher in clothing and 37% higher in food and drink. Clothing spend also rose 13% across merchants signalling that Singles Day promotions, or early Black Friday deals, may be reaching beyond Asia.
Central and Eastern Europe was the strongest region outside APAC, with shoppers spending 24% more on the day and increases of 36% in Poland, 30% in Croatia, 26% in the Czech Republic and 23% in both Slovakia and Lithuania. Elsewhere in Europe the picture was more mixed: spending was broadly flat, with Italy (+19%) and Norway (+52%) the exceptions. 
Rory O’Neill, Chief Marketing Officer at Checkout.com, said: "Singles' Day is the first real test of the peak season, and last year's data shows exactly where shoppers are ready to spend: fashion, department stores and general retail. Merchants who get their promotions and their checkout right will be best placed to turn that early demand into lasting growth through Black Friday and beyond."
In the run-up to Black Friday 2026, Checkout.com is helping businesses turn peak-season demand into revenue. The company’s upcoming campaign will spotlight the trends, insights and practical strategies shaping the world’s biggest shopping moment, so merchants can prepare with confidence, deliver valuable experiences for their customers, and use AI to optimise every transaction.
*All increases compare Singles' Day (11 November 2025) with the daily average of the preceding seven days (4-10 November 2025), based on payment volume processed by Checkout.com. APAC and UK figures are derived from the sales region of the merchant, not the location of the shopper, while individual country figures and the CEE figures are derived from the issuing country of the cardholder.

title: Axiology Secures Approval to Expand Investment Services, Simplifying Access to Tokenised Funds
summary:
Axiology, a regulated European capital markets infrastructure provider, has received approval from the Bank of Lithuania to extend its EU investment firm authorisation, allowing it to provide additional brokerage services alongside its existing trading and settlement infrastructure. The expansion is designed to simplify institutional access to tokenised financial instruments, including money market funds (MMFs).
The expanded licence authorises Axiology to receive and transmit orders and execute them on behalf of clients, adding two significant investment services to its existing licence. These permissions allow Axiology to receive clients’ investment instructions, execute transactions on their behalf or pass orders to their other venues and counterparties.
Combined with its existing permissions, Axiology can support the key stages of the investment process within a single regulated firm, from handling orders to through to trading, settlement and custody. 
The expansion is particularly relevant for corporate treasury teams looking to invest in tokenised MMFs. Axiology can now handle investment orders and facilitate subscriptions and redemptions with fund providers, alongside its existing settlement and custody services. This reduces the need for separate brokerage arrangements and makes it easier for institutions to access and manage tokenised investments.
Marius Jurgilas, CEO at Axiology, comments: “Tokenisation has the potential to make capital markets much more efficient, but there’s little benefit in simplifying the technology if investors still have to navigate a complicated process to access it. For treasury teams, that means dealing with multiple providers to place an order, complete a transaction and manage their holdings.
“Extending our authorisation is a deliberate step towards bringing the full investment process under one regulated roof. By combining brokerage with our existing infrastructure, we can make it easier for clients to access and manage these investments through one regulated provider.”
The expansion comes amid strong growth in tokenised MMFs. According to the European Central Bank, their global market capitalisation grew by around 110% during 2025, reaching approximately €7 billion by February 2026. While still a small segment of the wider money market fund industry, this growth is increasing the need for regulated infrastructure that can support broader institutional adoption.
Axiology has been authorised to operate a DLT Trading and Settlement System under the EU DLT Pilot Regime since July 2025. It was also amongst the initial DLT operators onboarded for Pontes, launched by the Eurosystem in September 2026 to enable wholesale transactions in tokenised financial instruments to settle in central bank money. It is a member of the Appia Contact Group, which supports the evolution of Pontes and the Eurosystem’s longer-term work on a European tokenised financial ecosystem.

title: Global Cross-Border Payment Targets Risk Masking Delays and High Costs, Warns The Payments Association
summary:
Global targets for cross-border payments risk masking delays and high costs experienced by customers, according to a new report from The Payments Association, a trade group for the payments industry.
The report, Rethinking Cross-border Payments Targets, was developed in collaboration with Payall, a cross-border payments infrastructure provider. It examines whether existing measures of progress accurately reflect the experience of businesses and consumers making international payments.
The Financial Stability Board (FSB) established the targets in 2021 as part of a G20-backed effort to make cross-border payments faster, cheaper, more accessible and more transparent, with most due to be met by the end of 2027.
While recognising the progress made so far, The Payments Association’s Cross-Border Working Group notes that nearly one in five monitored corridors (18.3%) still had average retail payment costs above the FSB’s 3% threshold in 2025, down from 24.1% the year before. Global averages alone cannot show where payments remain slow or expensive, the group argues.
The Payments Association recommends that future targets place greater emphasis on the complete payment journey and performance in individual corridors, including whether funds reach recipients at the expected time and cost.
It also proposes making safety and security an explicit part of the framework, alongside the existing targets for cost, speed, access and transparency. Faster payments can leave less time to detect and stop fraud, yet safety is not currently measured as a standalone target. Proposed measures cover payment fraud and misdirection, fund recovery, financial crime controls and operational and cyber resilience.
Emma Banymandhub, CEO of The Payments Association, said: “Businesses and consumers care what a payment costs and when it arrives, and that is what we need to measure. The international targets have helped bring the industry together, and we’ve seen real progress. The next step is to build on that work by looking at the whole payment journey and making safety and security part of how we measure success.”
Gary Palmer, founder and CEO of Payall Payment Systems, said: “"There has been enormous investment and innovation in cross-border payments, yet they too often remain unacceptably costly, slow and opaque. The targets established in 2021 gave us important, measurable ambitions, but we now need to ask whether progress is being measured in the right way. What matters is not whether one component has improved, but whether the payment experience for all parties has improved.”

content: A new report from The Payments Association warns that global cross-border payment targets risk masking ongoing delays and high costs for customers. Developed with Payall, the report suggests that current global averages fail to show where international payments remain slow or expensive. It recommends focusing on individual corridors, the complete payment journey, and adding safety and security as explicit targets alongside cost, speed, access, and transparency.

title: Avaloq launches Avaloq Mosaic, a modular platform for wealth managers
summary:
Avaloq, a global wealth technology firm and part of NEC Corporation, today announced its entry into the U.S. market with the launch of Avaloq Mosaic, a modular platform for wealth managers seeking to modernize investment technology without requiring a full platform replacement.
Avaloq Mosaic connects investment data and portfolio processes across existing systems, helping firms introduce new capabilities progressively. Many U.S. wealth managers rely on complex technology environments built up over years of growth and acquisitions. This can make it harder to support personalized investment strategies at scale, respond rapidly to market developments and adopt AI-enabled operating models.
Avaloq Mosaic debuts in the U.S. with two core capabilities, Portfolio IQ and Allocator. Portfolio IQ provides a real-time investment view, consolidating holdings, transactions and portfolio information across multiple accounts, custodians and other sources. Allocator translates investment strategies into portfolios across large and complex client books, supporting portfolio construction, personalization and ongoing management at scale.
Together, Portfolio IQ and Allocator provide a connected foundation for investment data and portfolio management. The broader Avaloq Mosaic offering also includes Agent Connect, which provides firms’ AI tools with governed access to verified investment data. Avaloq will expand the offering with additional capabilities, including Tax for tax-aware investment management, Asset Servicing for position keeping and securities-event administration, and Lending for margin and securities-backed lending decisions.
Built for complex wealth environments, Avaloq Mosaic combines a composable, cloud-native and API-first architecture with the governance and operating discipline required by large financial institutions.
Martin Greweldinger, Group CEO of Avaloq, said: “The U.S. is the world’s largest and one of the most sophisticated wealth markets, with distinct demands on the technology supporting advisors and clients. For more than four decades, Avaloq has built and operated technology for wealth managers across major global markets. With Avaloq Mosaic, we are bringing that experience to the U.S., giving firms the flexibility to modernize their technology, make better use of their investment data and introduce new capabilities without replacing the systems they already rely on.”
Suzzanna Gill, President, Avaloq U.S., said: “U.S. wealth managers are balancing greater scale with increasingly sophisticated portfolios and rising client demand for faster, more personalized insight, often on technology infrastructures built over many years. The opportunity for firms is to connect investment data with processes they already have, so they can modernize where it creates the greatest business impact.”
Avaloq has established a U.S. leadership team with experience across wealth management, brokerage, advisory technology and business transformation. Gill has extensive experience in wealth management transformation and building technology-enabled businesses in the U.S. Joel Lewis, Managing Director, U.S. Region, brings experience spanning self-directed brokerage, scaled advisory and full-service wealth management, with a focus on product strategy, transformation and business development.
Avaloq supports more than 170 financial institutions globally and reinvests 20% of its software revenue in research and development. Its technology helps wealth managers and private banks automate processes, streamline operations and manage complexity at scale.

title: Light Frame Raises $5.1 Million to Modernise Private Banking Technology
summary:
Light Frame, the financial technology company providing modern core banking and portfolio management software for the wealth industry, today announced the successful closing of an oversubscribed $5.1 million Seed financing round.
The round was led by Fortino Ventures, with participation from Sidekick Partners, Tenity, Chamaeleon, and AltaIR Capital, alongside existing investors including Rogue Venture Partners, New Stack Ventures, and Studio Alpha.
The financing comes amid growing institutional adoption of Light Frame's technology across EMEA, where the company is supporting live client operations and expanding its presence in the private banking and wealth management markets.
Revolutionizing the wealth industry
Across the wealth industry, institutions continue to rely on technology built on architectures developed decades ago.  The result is an industry constrained by infrastructure that is too slow to implement, too costly to operate, and not capable enough to meet the industry’s evolving needs.
Light Frame has developed a new generation of core banking and portfolio management technology designed specifically for the wealth industry. Engineered in Switzerland, the platform combines comprehensive banking and investment capabilities with a cloud-native, API-first architecture designed around artificial intelligence. Through embedded AI capabilities and its secure interoperability layer, the platform enables institutions to automate complex operations, improve employee productivity and deliver more sophisticated client services. Its fully modular design allows institutions to modernise individual components of their existing infrastructure or adopt a complete solution, significantly reducing implementation timelines, operational complexity and total cost of ownership.
 “Light Frame delivers foundational technology with the sophistication institutions require,” said Schuyler Weiss, Co-founder and CEO of Light Frame. “AI is redefining what technology can deliver, but the realization of its potential in the Wealth industry is dependent on the underlying infrastructure. The architecture must be designed around this future, without compromising the security, resilience and trust fundamental to banking. In Fortino and our broader investor group, we have found partners who share our ambition to build that foundation for the next generation of wealth management.”
Light Frame was founded in 2024 by Schuyler Weiss, founder and former CEO of Alpian, Switzerland's first cloud-native private bank; Mathieu Clément, Alpian's former COO and CIO; and technologists Philippe Kernevez and Gregory Bataille. The founding team brings direct experience building and operating a regulated Swiss bank, including the challenges associated with implementing and maintaining traditional banking infrastructure.
"We are excited to back a team that is exceptionally credible in this space,” said Hugh Phelan, Investment Manager at Fortino Ventures “Schuyler and the team have run a regulated Swiss bank on the kind of infrastructure they are now replacing. Few founders in wealth technology have lived the problem this closely, and fewer still have the technical depth to solve it. For a bank, moving sensitive data and live operations onto a new platform is an act of trust, and this team has earned the right to ask for it."
The funding will support continued investment in the platform, expansion of implementation and client delivery capacity, and the growth of Light Frame's commercial activities, initially focused on EMEA.

title: OpenPayd Hits $107 Million Annual Recurring Revenue as Fiat and Stablecoin Business Expands
summary:
OpenPayd, a leading provider of financial infrastructure, reached an annual recurring revenue of $107 million in October, following 44% year-on-year revenue growth to $25.4 million in the second quarter of its FY27 financial year. The results reflect continued demand across its fiat and stablecoin infrastructure.
The results reflect continued expansion across OpenPayd’s established fiat infrastructure alongside a growing contribution from stablecoin orchestration. Fiat infrastructure accounted for 70% of first-half revenue growth, with stablecoin orchestration contributing the remaining 30%.
 
OpenPayd launched its stablecoin infrastructure in May 2025, extending its platform across blockchain rails and enabling businesses to move between fiat and digital assets through a single infrastructure layer. First-half revenue from stablecoin orchestration increased from $0.5 million to $3.9 million year-on-year, as the infrastructure entered its second year of operation.
 

Iana Dimitrova, Chief Executive Officer at OpenPayd, said: “Passing $100 million in annual recurring revenue is an important milestone for OpenPayd. What’s particularly significant is where that growth is coming from – continued expansion across our fiat business, alongside a meaningful contribution from stablecoin orchestration.
 
“Our clients don’t need to make a bet on which rail will win. They need interoperable infrastructure that allows them to move and manage money across both, and use what works best for each flow. These results show how that approach is translating into growth, as existing clients do more with OpenPayd and new clients come onto the platform.”
 
Customers onboarded during FY27 contributed 34% of first-half banking and payments revenue growth. Stablecoin orchestration accounted for 32% of revenue from those new customers, reflecting its role in attracting new business as well as supporting existing clients.
 
As of October 2026, OpenPayd served more than 1,260 corporate clients and processed more than $360 billion in annualised transaction volume. Client balances held exceeded $1 billion, reflecting the scale of activity supported across the platform.
